item.title: How to Play Levia in Silver Age
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|competitive

How to Play Levia in Silver Age

Satiate your hunger with Karol's guide to the returning Shadow Brute!

By Karol Ruszkiewicz

|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Levia has shown up as a huge contender this Silver Age season, securing three placements in the Top 8 thanks to the efforts of Jacob Clements, Francesco Giorgio, and Kilian Schellekens. I've scoured through these decklists to find which cards are must-includes and what tech the different players have sprinkled in.

Levia already had some great common and rare cards in the past. Dread Screamer, Boneyard Marauder, Endless Maw, and Graveling Growl have all been incredible at punching through raw damage. However, the way these work, it takes some time to get enough cards into the graveyard, let alone enough 6-power attack action cards to consistently play these out while satisfying Levia's blood debt.

In terms of previous equipment, Hooves of the Shadowbeast has been a monster of a leg piece, being extremely flexible in granting not only an attack go again, but also an action point as long as you have a card to banish. That's it. Banish a 6-power card and you can convert your boots into a clean action point. Beaten Trackers...but better?

More recently, Compendium of Rathe introduced further power cards in the form of Embraforged Gauntlet, Engulfing Shadows, and Pound of Flesh.

On the Brute side, we also received some top-tier pieces of equipment that play really well into Levia's game plan. Buzzard Helm helps fix awkward hands, such as drawing four reds, while also filling up the graveyard to enable the old-school Shadow Brute attacks.

Predatory Plating also offers great defensive value and a precious resource when it matters. And it can matter a lot.

Levia's curve often uses 2-cost cards with go again, meaning two blues are perfect for playing out three of these in a row, often performing her iconic attack for 6, then 6, then 6. However, sometimes you're only able to attack twice, and 4 can be an awkward amount of pitch. This is why we see these lists include Vigorous Smashup in yellow and blue, with some running all six available copies. Vigor and top-deck manipulation are crucial for smoothing out certain turns, especially when combined with the toys Levia just received in Usurp the Shadow Throne...

So what makes Levia so good all of a sudden?

Firstly, it's the new attacks.

Big Bonkers

What's better than some over-rate attacks? A whole lot more over-rate attacks! Not only that, but ones that don't require a busy graveyard to get going.

Feeding Frenzy and Feasting Shadowbeast are all-star attacks that not only match the efficiency of the Monarch attacks, but are also much easier to enable. Their effects are satisfied by any banish, not just their own. This means they make great follow-up cards and can also be enabled by cards like Hex Gauntlet and Cleave the Heavens.

Gates to i'Arathael

Cleave the Heavens isn't just a pretty face. It creates one of the most important components of Levia's toolkit: Gates to i'Arathael, a token that unlocks "free" cards from banish. As the game goes on, you'll have more and more juicy targets for these Gates, allowing you to throw out attacks with unparalleled efficiency.

Being able to convert a single blue into a Feasting Shadowbeast for 8 while satisfying blood debt is incredible, especially in Silver Age. Gates are particularly effective against slower decks that give you time to set up big turns and the space to build a hefty banish zone. I recommend leaning further into setting up Gates with cards like Rites of Nightfall, Countdown to Extinction, and more copies of Cleave the Heavens if your local metagame likes to take it slow.

Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger

The big demon makes his way into Silver Age! Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger offers an amazing package against a wide range of decks. Cards like Goremass Summoning, Beckoning Hunger, and Rumbling Hunger are the main ways to get the demon into the arena, and that is one scary on-hit. If your opponent lets this one through, it can take over the game.

While Gates offer a similar effect, not having to pitch that extra resource and having the effect on tap means you can continue playing free cards from banish, as long as you feed the beast, that is.

Blasmophet's upkeep requires you to continue banishing Shadow cards. Luckily, on your turn you're most likely doing that anyway to satisfy your hero ability. However, it's a bit trickier to do so on your opponent's turn. Some cards fulfill this condition themselves. Cleave the Heavens, Embraforged Gauntlet, and Engulfing Shadows all banish Shadow cards in one form or another.

Some cards also benefit from having a Blasmophet in play. The most played one is Consuming Command, a power play if you have it in your banish zone while controlling a Blasmophet. For 1 resource, you get to attack for 6 with go again, and the best thing is that if you continue to load it with graveyard-banishing effects, you can continue to attack with it. Most lists run only one copy, as that seems to be all you need to get the loop going.

Metagaming

There are a few cards that stood out to me, as they made some lists but not others.

Kilian's build seems the most resilient to fatigue strategies. Including two copies of Howl from Beyond opens up a constant loop of power. You play out the Howl, buff up your attack, then banish it from the graveyard with a Dread Screamer or Boneyard Marauder.

Jacob Clements is a big fan of Agility. Including a Test of Agility and Clash of Agility means that, as long as he can win those clashes, he can make these already incredibly efficient attacks even better by giving them go again. Smashback Alehorn offers even more go again and extra power, making it a great setup card for creating explosive turns.

Another point of contention is whether the lists should run Consuming Lash or Consuming Strength. As a general rule of thumb, I'd say go again is more likely to be useful against slower decks, while the extra +2 power pairs nicely with on-hit attacks like Rumbling Hunger and Beckoning Hunger, especially against aggressive decks that don't want to be defending.

Closing Thoughts

Despite just entering this new metagame, these players have turned up with incredibly tuned decks and a strategy for anything their opponents might throw at them.

I hope you got plenty of useful information on how to pilot Levia, because she is not only a highly competitive deck, but also a delightful puzzle to solve each and every game.

item.title: The Best-Selling Cards in Disney Lorcana Right Now - September 2026
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|finance

The Best-Selling Cards in Disney Lorcana Right Now - September 2026

Rapunzel? What is this, 2025?!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

It's been a hectic month for Disney Lorcana as the road to Hyperia City marches forward.We're about to enter a wondrous world blending music and art with the fantastical whimsy of heroes and princesses, introducing the much-beloved Coco to the game for the very first time. The setis also stuffed with fan-favourite franchises like Zootopia, Gargoyles and A Goofy Movie, and sounsurprisingly has been stealing most of the spotlight as we get closer to release. 

But we've also had a ton of play to follow at both the local level and tournament tables. Between the North American Championship, European Championship and Brazilian Championship, the metagame has been shifting almost every week. In fact, I still can't confidently tell you what the best deck in the format is! 

Well, you know what they say: When in doubt, trust Frank Karsten. 

But clearly the community has its own plans! Between speculatory purchases that are synergistic with new reveals from Hyperia City, a continued reinvigoration of the collecting aspect of the game and a variety of viable decks at the top of the metagame, it's been incredibly fun to chunk though the bestsellers data this month. 

You wanna see what everybody has been buying? I thought you might. Let's chat about the best-selling cards in Disney Lorcana throughout September 2026. 

#10 Lilo & Stitch - Fun-Loving Friends

The dynamic duo may have been crashing in price, but that hasn't slowed interest in the Amber Steel lynchpin. Lilo & Stitch - Fun-Loving Friends provides an absurd rate on an early character that's more than happy to shift in and sing He Hurled His Thunderbolt. 

The card isn't flashy, but it doesn't need to be. All the numbers here are great, and the only reason it isn't seeing more play is because it's ink-locked to Amber Steel. As the format adjusts to allow one of the better OG combinations to flourish, we'll see plenty of Lilo & Stitch. It makes sense that players are grabbing them while they're cheap! 

#9 Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty

On the other end of the spectrum, Milo Thatch has been getting his hands dirty. The card continues to be on the up-and-up as Amber Emerald Songs/Circle of Life and the infamous Emerald Sapphire Mouse House continue to find their footing at the tournament tables. 

Ward is such a big draw in an interactive format, but a three-pip threat that's also forcing discards and generating cards is a whole different beast. I'm glad to see Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty finally having his moment in the sun and I'm not expecting it to end post-Hyperia City. In fact, ink drops probably just elevate what Milo is capable of. 

#8 Gaston - Superior Archer

It's a continued fall from grace for Gaston - Superior Archer, who already stumbled from the best-selling card in Attack of the Vine! to a second-place finish last month. However, this isn't because the card became bad overnight — quite the opposite. I just think that most players have secured their copies of Gaston at this point. 

We're still shooting down many of the biggest threats in Core Constructed with a well-stated, inkable bow. Much like Lilo & Stitch (who conveniently support Gaston), I expect the play rate for this card to only increase as we enter metagames where it truly shines. 

If anything, you should see this as a sign that you're lacking behind if you haven't spent your three bucks to pick these up yet. 

#7 Winnie the Pooh & Piglet - Hunny Mages

This is adorable to see and brings me joy. I'm curious how much of this acceleration of sales for Winnie the Pooh & Piglet - Hunny Mages comes from [Format Coconut], where it's even easier to find yourself with multiple ink colors in play.

There's also a chance that cards from the Hundred-Acre Wood are seeing an uptick of sales to align with their hundred-year anniversary, which sees several news books releasing about our honey-loving friend. Otherwise, I can only see this as another signpost of the popularity of duo cards, which have consistently appeared on our bestseller lists since they were released in Attack of the Vine!. 

I'll be curious to see if this one can hold the momentum going forward. 

#6 Woody & Buzz Lightyear - Best Buddies

Another duo rocking the list, Woody & Buzz Lightyear - Best Buddies feels like its waiting for the right moment to strike at the tournament tables. Amber Emerald Toys doesn't quite have the oomph to hold its own with other archetypes in those inks right now, but it feels like it's only a matter of time. After all, toys are still a relatively new thing. 

That said, this is yet another endorsement of the increasing casual side of the collector's market in Disney Lorcana. Woody and Buzz aren't worth a fortune in their base rarity, but Disney fans simply want to own cards that feature their favorite characters and that's a lovely thing. 

#5 Mushu - Stealthy Dragon

Attack of the Vine's most expensive legendary continues to move units month-on-month, but it's a significant fall from first to fifth. I'm sure the previous sales numbers play a part in this slow decline, but the card has also fallen out of favor from some Emerald Steel and Emerald Amethyst pilots. 

That said, it's still a powerhouse. Mushu - Stealthy Dragon is a must-answer threat that has warped the format around the format, and it'll likely continue to create those metagame vortexes at several points until it rotates. 

You're just going to want to own copies of Mushu at some point in the next twelve months, and under ten bucks seems a good time to make sure that happens. 

#4 Mickey Mouse - Bob Cratchit

Okay, I'm gonna try to keep my personal biases in check on this one. There's definitelyno need to call anyone a "monster" or some other name... and it definitely doesn't get worse further up this list. 

If you couldn't tell, I'm not the biggest fan of Emerald Sapphire Mouse House. I can't deny that the deck is exactly that — a house. Quick lore and Ward characters are a surefire recipe for game wins, and we're seeing more players than ever lean on Mickey Mouse - Bob Cratchit as the best rodent to enable the namesake threat: Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo.

The base rarity is up an eyewatering 756% in the last thirty days as copies on the market start to thin. If you want the epic variant, you're looking at $33 a copy at this point. Bruh.

#3 Dr. Bushroot - Evil Botanist

Disney Lorcana players out here showing their true colors in September... and they're green and blue. 

Dr. Bushroot - Evil Botanist is one of the standard Ward options available to Emerald Sapphire Mouse House, ripping away the limited tools the opponent has to challenge you as they desperately try to shut down your removal-proof-huge-pip board of characters. It's not flashy, but it achieves that role incredibly well. 

At seventy cents, it's hard to complain really. Dr. Bushroot will continue to sell en-masse for as long as more players gravitate towards Emerald Sapphire for their events. Will Hyperia City add more tools for the archetype? We'll have to wait and see. 

#2 Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo

Of course. Who else could it be? 

You don't become the namesake of a deck without making some cheddar. Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo continue to climb month-on-month as their budget-friendly deck flourishes in popularity. 

We previously saw the price of the card cascading towards $10 each as word got around, but it's currently at a much more affordable $4 despite the surge in popularity. I can't shake the feeling that this price chart is going to look like a rollercoaster by the end of the year. 

But who kept the lovable duo off the throne? Well. 

#1 Rapunzel - Escaping the Tower (Store Championship Promo)

That's right, specifically the Store Championship participant version of Rapunzel - Escaping the Tower. Strange, huh? 

This card has clearly become a target for speculation for a portion of the market that feel it is massively undervalued at just $2. It has sold almost double the amount of any other Disney Lorcana card on the TCGplayer marketplace this month, which is frankly an astounding stat. 

I can see the vision. The card has already seen a smattering of play in various Elinor - Renowned Diplomat decks and carries a stat line and type line that will continue to overperform. If you don't want to shell out thirty bucks for the shiny copies (or simply didn't win them) then there's no better version of the card to own. 

Heaven forbid we see a Shift Rapunzel in Hyperia City. That'd make this card go nuclear.

item.title: Basic Box Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)
item.description:
Pokémon|competitive

Basic Box Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)

It's anything but.

By Natalie Millar

|@nataliem9999
|

Published Oct 6, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Pokémon Deck Guides

Hello everyone! Basic Box is one of the mainstays of the current Standard format alongside Dragapult ex and it has one of the most flexible game plans available. There are a ton of different ways to build this archetype, so let's get into one of the more popular variants!

Basic Box Deck Guide

At its core, this is a Mega Kangaskhan ex deck. In almost every matchup, your primary game plan is to retreat into it early and use Run Errand to draw some cards, then attack with Rapid Fire Combo to put on early pressure. After the Kangaskhan goes down, you then proceed to attack with the other various options in this deck, including Lillie's Clefairy ex, Wellspring Mask Ogerpon ex and Raging Bolt ex. This deck takes on the aggressive role in most matchups and you have the ability to tech for almost any problem matchup.

This deck gets its main engine from a bunch of Basic Pokémon. You have three copies of Meowth ex to find Cyrano or Crispin early on, and Cyrano usually will find Latias ex to give all your Pokémon free retreat, the Kangaskhan itself to draw cards, then Teal Mask Ogerpon ex to start converting your Grass Energy into some extra cards in hand and Energy in play.

This version of Basic Box relies very heavily on Crispin to set up your attackers and to get tons of Energy in play for a late game Bellowing Thunder from Raging Bolt. You have four copies of Energy switch to assist with pivoting between your attackers and getting a surprise Torrential Pump to take multiple knockouts. Against Dragapult ex specifically, be careful of using Torrential Pump and opening yourself up to Unfair Stamp. Be aware of positions where you can also use Cruel Arrow to take advantage of a poor start from your opponent. Mew ex is one of the newest additions to this deck from the 30th Anniversary expansion which can help you with being more flexible. Mew ex lets you use Cruel Arrow early and then convert that Energy into either a Torrential Pump or a Bellowing Thunder and save your Energy Switches and Crispins for other attacks.

You still mostly need to attack with Mega Kangaskhan ex since your hand will quickly dry up if you aren't using Run Errand every turn, and if you attack with something else, it's ideal for that Pokémon to get knocked out so that you can draw cards with Flip the Script and Cruel Arrow. Iron Leaves also acts as a pseudo-card draw option in this deck because you can retreat to Kangaskhan, Run Errand and then use Rapid Vernier to get a knockout that turn. The Grass Energy will usually come from various Teal Dances throughout the game, and Iron Leaves often acts as a bridging attacker in the middle of the game.

Dragapult ex is one of the main reasons to play a deck like this. It's very difficult for your opponent to profitably attack into your Mega Kangaskhan because of its 300 HP, and you can usually go ahead by two Prize cards with Rapid Fire Combo. If they Phantom Dive your Kangaskhan and later set it up to get knocked out by the residual damage from Phantom Dive, you can use Energy Switch to save its Energy then use Chien-Pao's Snow Sink to remove the liability. This deck heavily relies on Area Zero Underdepths to fill out your board and get extra attackers into play, then Snow Sink to discard the Area Zero Underdepths and discard the extra Benched Pokémon, removing damaged Pokémon or Meowth exs from play. Lillie's Clefairy ex is your primary attacker against Dragapult ex, mostly because it gets knocked out immediately from a Phantom Dive, letting you use Run Errand and Flip the Script. Be careful of using Raging Bolt against Dragapult ex because they can play Unfair Stamp and Phantom Dive the Raging Bolt and not take a knockout, then if you miss the knockout on Dragapult, they can use Boss's Orders and take four Prize cards which will often result in you losing the game.

This deck does have a notable weakness against single-Prize decks, which is why this deck list includes a small package to defeat Alakazam. You can use Prime Catcher or Hero's Cape as the ACE SPEC, but if you can play Unfair Stamp against an Alakazam deck, you'll often set them back very far and can sometimes even out the Prize trade. The majority of Alakazam decks use Genesect SFA to prevent you from playing Unfair Stamp, but if they use Genesect, you can trap it active with Maractus JTG's Corner attack. Some Alakazam decks use Handheld Fan to prevent the Genesect from being trapped but with its Grass resistance, Maractus doesn't deal damage and doesn't trigger the Handheld Fan. You sit there and wait for your opponent to draw their whole deck and start looping Dudunsparce to prevent themselves from decking out, then you use Xerosic's Machinations to force them to discard their whole deck and win the game by attacking a few times. This does require you to play Unfair Stamp, Maractus, and Xerosic and not Prize any of these pieces but they completely swinging one of your worst matchups is very valuable.

This version with heavy Crispin is not the only viable version of Basic Box out there. There is another distinct version that is notably favoured by Japanese players that is more commonly referred to as "Turbo Ogerpon."

This deck focus much heavier on Teal Mask Ogerpon ex and doesn't use Crispin, instead just a ton of Grass Energy, Energy Switch and N's Plan to power up its additional attackers. You try to attack very early, sometimes on turn one, with Teal Mask Ogerpon ex, then power up additional attackers with Prism Energy. This deck doesn't use Mega Kangaskhan ex as much, and instead uses Lillie's Determination and Teal Dance to draw through your deck. This list is slightly worse against Dragapult ex since you can't attack with Mega Kangaskhan as easily and often give them a very profitable attack against either Teal Mask Ogerpon ex or Lillie's Clefairy ex. With only four copies of Prism Energy, this deck is also somewhat weak to Crushing Hammer, especially since you often need to find Prism Energy off an opposing Unfair Stamp. However, this version is notably faster and has a wider variety of attackers you can use. Both versions of Basic Box are very playable decks and I would expect to see either of them at any tournament you go to!

item.title: This Month in Japanese Yu-Gi-Oh (September 2026)
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|news

This Month in Japanese Yu-Gi-Oh (September 2026)

One of Yu-Gi-Oh's most unique card treatments comes to Japan.

By Samuel Frew

|

Published Oct 6, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Kia ora! September of 2026 was one of Yu-Gi-Oh's biggest months, as it was the month of Yu-Gi-Oh's 30th anniversary! There were two big new sets released, including more Grand Master Rares and the first Manga-Style cards, every format of the game had an updated Forbidden & Limited List following the World Championship, a bunch of promotional cards based on the manga became available, and a new episode of Yu-GI-Oh! CARD GAME THE CHRONICLES released.

Grand Manga Style

The Original Artwork Collection is easily one of the coolest sets to release this year in Japan. This set celebrates the Yu-Gi-Oh manga in a bunch of different ways, but the newest way is with Manga-Style cards!

Blue-Eyes White Dragon (colored Manga-Style)

Manga-Style cards are based on the presentation of Duel Monsters cards in the Yu-Gi-Oh manga. This means they are largely white-framed and have the artwork and printed effects (or lack-thereof in the case of cards like Blade Knight) that the card images had in the original manga. Many of the artworks in the manga were very different compared to the ones the Yu-Gi-Oh! Official Card Game uses, as the real cards instead often took their artwork from a dynamic pose that Kazuki Takahashi drew the monster in during the manga. 

There are 30 different Manga-Style cards in Original Artwork Collection, all of them cards from the original manga. They come in both monochrome and colored Ultra Rare and Secret Rare and they look fantastic; I just finished collecting the original manga myself, so seeing these has been a total treat.

Jinzo (Manga-Style)

The coolest thing about Manga-Style cards is that they're completely legal to use in the Yu-Gi-Oh! OCG. While their printed effects and card types might differ, the rules treat them the same as the real cards. We don't know if Manga-Style cards will be coming to the TCG yet, but it's worth pointing out that we did get the very similar oversized cards in Duel Overload a few years ago!

Exodia the Obliterator (extended art)

There are also 10 new extended are reimagined versions of classic Yu-Gi-Oh! monsters in Original Art Collection, which can also come as serialized Grand Master Rares. These include Exodia the Obliterator, which turns the tide of the duel when you draw it as Exodia the Forbidden One did for Yami Yugi, Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon, the God-Surpassing Servant, a Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon that combines the effects of all previous reimagined Ultimate Dragons, and Silent Magician, the Silent Fighter, a Silent Magician that resists destruction, draws cards to match your opponent's, and negates their Spells if you have a full hand.

Attribute Rejection

On top of that, Original Artwork Collection also has more reimagined cards and cards based on famous moments from the manga, like the two Evil Dragon Cards, a dangerous Chinese card game referenced in Xing Zhen Hu, and Attribute Rejection, the famous moment where Yami Yugi deliberately fused the incompatible Mammoth Graveyard with Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon. We even got another Dungeon Dice Monster at last in Knight of Twin Swords! Lastly, there's a bunch of reprints for the more modern versions of Yu-Gi-Oh! characters' decks, like Shining Sarcophagus, Millennium and Max Metalmorph.

Glory on the Victory!

The newest Deck-Build Pack also released at the beginning of September, with three new themes: Zenet, Raise Moon and Trirealm Rift.

Zenet Zwitch

The Zenet theme uses Normal Monsters and non-Effect Fusion Monsters to Ritual Summon their boss monsters with Pere-Zenet Em Heru and Am Duazenet, depending on the turn. Once you Ritual Summon a Zenet Ritual Monster with these cards, they equip a Normal Monster to the Ritual Monster you've Ritual Summoned, enabling the Zenet Ritual Monsters' powerful protective effects and fueling their Quick removal effects.

Zenetnakht Sphinx

Zenetnakht Sphinx for example can discard itself to search a Zenet card - the Zenet Rituals can also be Ritual Summoned from your graveyard - and sacrifices Normal Monster cards, including those equipped to it, to change the opponent's monsters face-down. Other Zenet Traps benefit from having both Ritual Monsters and Normal Monsters out to counter the opponent once the field is assembled.

Raise the Moon!

Then there's the Raise Moon theme, a Level 7 theme that bring the duel to their casino where the house rules prevent the players from searching, relying instead on the luck of the draw. Most Raise Moon monsters have effects to either Special Summon themselves when drawn or draw more cards, and many of their effects don't have limits on the number of times you can use them each turn!

Cielo, the Night Sky of Raise Moon - No More Bets!

The Raise Moon Xyz Monsters control the house, with Cielo, the Night Sky of Raise Moon - No More Bets! turning your opponent's search effects into draws and stanchly resisting efforts to get rid of her while she's in the Extra Monster Zone. The Raise Moons are backed up by Spell and Trap Cards that keep the deck loaded and drawing cards.

Invasion from the Trirealm Rift

The Trirealm Rift monsters looked at the Infernity's handless strategy and decided it wasn't extreme enough - they want you to play the game without any cards in your deck. Banish cards face-down from the top of your deck equal to a Trirealm Rift monster's Level whenever you summon it and you'll be able to access this pool of banished cards with the effects of the other Trirealm Rift monsters; the low-Level ones can summon themselves and the higher-Level monsters, while the high-Level ones fuel your supply of face-down banished cards.

With no cards in your deck and a high-Level Trirealm Rift out, their Field Spell prevents your opponent from taking any actions during your turn, and Trirealm Rift Darkness can prevent both players from drawing a card if there are at least forty banished face-down cards - a useful effect for impeding your opponent, but also to prevent yourself from losing with an empty deck!

Promotional Manga Cards

This month's VJump promotional card was another Dungeon Dice Monster, Armor Wizard Pazoo, Yugi's winning creature from his game with Duke Devlin in the manga. Pazoo's ability allowed it to transform into the Dungeon Master's sword and shield, defeating Duke's Orgoth the Relentless; likewise, this new card can equip to a monster and increase its ATK and DEF by 2100 each.
The Fall subscription bonus cards were also sent out this month. This time, three cards from the Yu-Gi-Oh! R manga were freshly released; Ted Banias' Assault Lion, who incorporates the effects of tons of his other cards to make a one-Tribute double-damage behemoth that can recur itself, and Gekko Tenma's Thoroughbred Elf and Power Connection, finally completing his winning strategy against Banias after the prior release of Armament Reincarnation.

White Witch of the Winter Raven

This month's episode of Yu-Gi-Oh! CARD GAME THE CHRONICLES continued the Sinful Spoils arc, with Diabellstar the Black Witch continuing to delight as a character as she deals with Snake-Eyes Poplar and the Goblin Bikers, only for matters to further complicate after her long-lost sister, Diabellze the Original Sinkeeper shows up. 

Diabellze is also getting what appears to be a post-Sinful Spoils theme in Immortal Phoenix, the Winter Ravens - I'll have more to say on those next month!

Shifting on the Banlist

Japan's latest Forbidden & Limited list was revealed this month right before ours, and there was a lot of overlap and hits to top tier decks.

Just as we would, the OCG banned PSY-Framelord Omega and Dimension Shifter, but they also banned Supreme King Dragon Starving Venom, a hit that's long been enforced in the TCG. A ton of cards from Elfnotes, Kewl Tunes and Toons were Limited as well, and problem cards like Perfectron Hydradrive Dragon and Appointer of the Red Lotus (which is already banned in the TCG) also got Limited. 

The OCG also finally unbanned Premature Burial, which is likely to make its way down the list every so often, as unbanned cards that prove safe enough do so. Quite a few Semi-Limited cards made their way off the banlist this way, and the errata'd Mind Master and Elder Entity Norden skipped the Semi-Limited list from Limited and went straight to Unlimited. The Fallen & The Virtuous and Sky Striker Mobilize - Engage! both went to Semi-Limited as well from Unlimited, so we'll see how they go. And of course, Maxx "C" escaped notice again, remaining in Limited.

It's not often that we get two big sets in a month, but such are the demands of the 30th anniversary of Yu-Gi-Oh! Immortal Phoenix will release in Japan next month, bringing more new cards and strategies to the game and setting their post-banlist slate truly in motion.

item.title: The 12 Magic: The Gathering Cards I'm Excited To Play From Reality Fracture
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|competitive

The 12 Magic: The Gathering Cards I'm Excited To Play From Reality Fracture

What doesn't grow, dies. And what dies grows the tarmogoyf (in Standard).

By Seth Manfield

|@SethManfield
|

Published Oct 6, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

As we travel into the Echoverse with Reality Fracture, there are several cards that jump out to me for various formats. Today, I'll be going over my highly-anticipated picks from the set, as well as the formats I expect to see them played in. Several of the highlights here include reprints with a storied history, and it will be very interesting to see how they impact the current state of the game.

Tarmogoyf

Let's start with a card that was first printed in Future Sight, and has become a staple across multiple formats for the past two decades. Tarmogoyf used to be a card that seemingly most decks in Modern Constructed were playing, but as the format has shifted and power levels have changed, Tarmogoyf has found itself on the outside looking in regarding Modern as of late. 

However, what Tarmogoyf means for Standard Constructed is a completely new and unprecedented question that hasn't been posed for many years. I personally feel Tarmogoyf will be at home in the current Standard format, and I'm looking forward to building a Golgari Midrange deck that can fill up the graveyard with various card types early in the game. The power level of Tarmogoyf is often determined by the surrounding pieces of interaction played alongside it, as well as what types of removal the opponent is playing.

Bloodline Recollector

Bloodline Recollector feels like a card that has a lot of potential, but will only fit in a very specific sacrifice-style deck that can consistently prepare it. The ability to have a repeatable Ancestral Recall in black sounds like a nice way to dominate the late game. Decks that successfully utilize Bloodline Recollector will need to flood the board with creatures that are easy to sacrifice for value, and have a way to gain life to make the lifeloss from Ancestral Craving bearable. I expect to see Bloodline Recollector in multiple formats, though time will tell if it's strong enough to break through into a top-tier strategy. 

Enlightened Confidant

Who doesn't like a competitive deck focused on lifegain? While Enlightened Confidant doesn't necessarily need a ton of other lifegain to support it, the more lifegain effects the better this card becomes. I have taken Soul Sisters-type strategies to major events before, and this is a card that is definitely good enough to see play in that style deck. Lifegain decks usually play mostly cards with low mana costs, likely turning any surveil into card draw.

Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes

Creating Jace planeswalker tokens with the Empower Jace ability is one of the signature mechanics in Reality Fracture, and it's going to be very interesting to see how this works out competitively. I personally think the ability to create planeswalkers for a low cost seems very powerful. The card advantage the Jace will create is a big deal, and Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes is able to Empower Jace for the easy cost of a landfall trigger. Not to mention, this will work very nicely alongside with the various Fetch Lands.

Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes is pretty underrated in my opinion, and I expect to see it a lot in Commander, Standard, or even Modern as there are strong arguments for power level here. The Jace token is mostly a way to draw an extra card each turn, with the surveil ability being an added bonus. Protecting the token is somewhat important, but with Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes in play creating a replacement Jace token shouldn't be difficult.

Chandra, Torch of Defiance

Chandra, Torch of Defiance was a format-defining card in the Kaladesh era of Standard, though I don't expect it to have as significant an impact in the current format. However, I do like this card and expect it will be useful as a way for red decks to play a longer game plan if they want to. I personally love a good midrange red deck, and it feels somewhat difficult to build a powerful one right now.

Extrapolate the Impossible

Having ways to access your sideboard is generally a good thing, and I wish we generally had more "Wish" cards that can fetch spells from the sideboard such as this one. I can see Extrapolate the Impossible working well in a combo-focused deck that has redundant pieces like a reanimator strategy, or it could be used to find win conditions in a mana ramp deck. Expect to see Extrapolate the Impossible used in best-of-one play on MTG Arena as there isn't a punishment for using sideboard slots on searchable targets. For traditional best of three, managing your options for what to find with this (versus more traditional sideboard choices) will be important.

Stingcaster Mage

Snapcaster Mage in a non-blue color would feel like a bold choice in a different era of Magic, but we have seen the impact of Snapcaster Mage across basically every format in Magic now, so we mostly know what we are getting with Stingcaster Mage. Figuring out the best way to utilize this card will be tricky, but it definitely has a home in the right deck. 

The Mage coming with haste is also relevant, though this isn't the ideal play on turn two, as the value comes from the opportunity to flashback a spell. Having inexpensive spells (for instance Lightning Bolt) that can be re-cast will be very important for older formats. Stingcaster Mage could fit nicely in a red midrange deck, or a deck geared towards filling up the graveyard.

The Echoverse Fulcrum

I see The Echoverse Fulcrum as a card that artifact decks may want to search for, or play in combination with other artifact or colorless synergies. Being able to draw and discard a card upon the Fulcrum entering is pretty valuable, and there aren't many ways to answer the board with an artifact. The Echoverse Fulcrum isn't going to make massive competitive waves in my opinion, but should have a home somewhere. I personally love silver bullet artifacts, whether that means finding them with a Karn, the Great Creator or searching for one with Repurposing Bay.

Lich's Relic

Normally I'm not one to play equipment, but Lich's Relic does seem exceptionally strong. Getting reasonably-costed removal of any creature or planeswalker, and is also an equipment with a reasonable equip cost is a good package to have. It's hard to say exactly where we will see Lich's Relic, as the types of decks that want a black equipment plus removal effect are somewhat difficult to build. That said, I look forward to seeing where Lich's Relic ends up fitting in.

Vigorbloom Charm

Vigorbloom Charm should work well in Selesnya Midrange or Landfall as a versatile removal spell that can also be converted into a fresh card, or even protecting your best creature. Like many other cards in Reality Fracture, the power here is the flexibility of use. Vigorbloom Charm is never going to be a bad card in any matchup because of the versatility it brings to the table, and that means it is less of a liability against control strategies for instance. Vigorbloom Charm should see play in both Standard and more casual Commander formats.

Fatehold Charm

The Charms in Reality Fracture are quite strong overall, though in the case of Fatehold Charm, the first mode which draws a card and Empowers Jace 2 seems like the best of the bunch. Empower Jace overall has the potential to be very impactful, to the point I'm actually concerned this could be too strong for competitive play. The ability to pump your team with Fatehold Charm is also quite nice, yet it is easily the worst mode on the card. This is a card that could certainly make waves if the Empower Jace mechanic is as strong as advertised.

The Theorist, Jace Beleren

Planeswalkers are a large part of Reality Fracture, and in particular Jace. Jace Beleren is one of the five original planeswalkers (dubbed the Lorwyn Five), so I love seeing Jace Beleren returning in a new form. The Theorist, Jace Beleren strikes me as the right power level for a four mana planeswalker for competitive play. The passive ability of drawing a card on each opponent's turn is going to be exceptionally good in multiplayer formats, and I could see the card become game-warping due to the overwhelming card advantage it provides.

For Standard, I also expect The Theorist, Jace Beleren will be of interest to control and midrange decks. The Illusion tokens can protect your planeswalker, and four mana to bounce a creature or artifact, drawing a card, and having a planeswalker still on the battlefield is a good rate. Getting to six loyalty will be tough, but being able to turn the Illusion tokens into big threats as a way to close out the game seems pretty fun.

item.title: Weiss SchwarzThe 10 Cards Everybody Wants From GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE Vol. 2
item.description:
Weiss Schwarz|collecting

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants From GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE Vol. 2

By Drew Knapp

|@FenrirRex
|

Published Oct 6, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE makes its return to Weiss Schwarz, and it is a truly triumphant return. The IP is beloved by collectors in particular, in no small part because many of those collectors have a broad crossover with the gacha game that the set is based around. That said, there are a lot of highly playable, build around cards waiting in the set for anyone who is just as interested in playing as collecting. Let's take a look at what people are hoping to pull, topped by the highest rarities that you can find in your GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE Vol. 2 packs.

#10 "Feather All-Range" Ein (SSP)

We're opening the list with an all-star, if one that might be very mildly controversial. The new set is genuinely stacked with a lot of highly-playable Level 3 cards, and "Feather All-Range" Ein may struggle to make the list for some. The flexibility of her kit, however, is entirely undeniable, enough that I'll give her the bump here. Her cute design and a markedly cute signature join to up the value of this card, and I would strongly consider bumping her up in your own estimations.

#9 "Shackles of Destiny" Arcana (SSP)

The mystical, tarot card aesthetic on "Shackles of Destiny" Arcana is very high on my list of positive vibes in the set. I am similarly a huge fan of early game effects that can generate some late game value. It turns out consistently being able to return cards to hand can put in some work, and I feel shackled to the need to play this card. I'll be happy to play any version, but the rare SSP variant is what you'll be hoping to roll.

#8 Privaty - Banquet Princess (SSP)

Privaty is another recurring name for anyone who played with the first GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE set, and I love to see a fan-favorite. Privaty joins the stack of powerful Level 0 characters that help you set up your future plays. There are plenty of cards that help you do this, but previous few of them look anywhere near as good as the SSP variant of Privaty - Banquet Princess.

#7 Mihara: Bonding Chain (SSP)

A surprisingly number of the higher rarity cards in the set are less fanservicey than one might expect from the IP, but Mihara: Bonding Chain jumps out as an immediate example of the game's allure. You can't really ignore the (lack of) costuming and implications with the chain theme, and its clear that the designers have a bit of a sense of humor with how they integrated the heart signature. A lot of folks love having this kind of pinup design on display, so expect to see a lot of this card.

#6 "Plot Spoiler" Grave (SSP)

I love a good antagonist, and Grave is one of the most interesting characters to come out of GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE as a whole. I'll admit that her character design has some weird choices (I will never understand giving an armored/cloaked character a bare midriff), but that aside I am a sucker for grim and gothic aesthetic. I'm not the only one, so combine that aesthetic with her potent role as a villain in the game, and the signature stamped version is something you should be beyond happy to pull.

#5 "Siren's Song" Little Mermaid (SEC)

If I were to put more weight just on how pretty the art on a card is, "Siren's Song" Little Mermaid would be very near the top, if not the absolute peak, of the list. That gorgeous art, lovely signature, and high rarity join the other upcoming SEC variants on the list to easily top the charts. I'll be interested in seeing which of the SEC variants gain or retain value, but they're all safely going to be of interest to collectors.

#4 "Glass Slippers. Full Contact" Cinderella (SEC)

While this isn't the Level 3 that I want to build around, that's not necessarily a commonly shared opinion. No, plenty of people will want to find the glass slippers to match this princess, and I really can't blame them even if it's less my style than another card we'll soon see on this list. With so many being bullish on this character (and she's also quite popular in the Gacha game itself!), I'm expecting her value to only go up.

#3 "Kill the Target" D: Killer Wife (SEC)

While almost any character in NIKKE could fall into the femme fatale archetype, basically no one does it better than D: Killer Wife. This classic assassin-type character is one of the best Level 0 cards to kick off your game plan, smoothing out your plays and looking absolutely killer while doing it. Top-tier aesthetic is joined by another beautiful signature, with this topping my personal list of cards I want to see from the set.

#2 Rapi: Red Hood (SEC)

The Rapi cards dominated community interest in the previous NIKKE set, so it's no surprise that she approaches the top of the charts for Vol. 2. This new Level 3 version of Rapi continues the trend, representing a powerful payoff for going all-in on the NIKKE game plan. A direct-damage dealing powerhouse, she's also a highly popular character and her rarest variant represents some serious money if you should find her waiting in your packs.

#1 Elegg: Boom and Shock (SEC)

The SEC variant of Elegg: Boom and Shock is the perfect combination of basically everything people are looking for from the set. This variant is as rare as they come, the art has some very strong appeal as an attractive slice-of-life scene, the character is extremely popular, and the card itself is good. It quite literally checks all the boxes I can think of for a chase piece (complete with no small amount of fanservice!), and you can bet I'll be shocked if I manage to pull a copy of this signature-stamped collector's item.

item.title: The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from 30th Celebration
item.description:
Pokémon|collecting

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from 30th Celebration

Pulls worth celebrating.

By Peter Day

|

Published Sep 15, 2026

|

10 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

It doesn't even feel like hyperbole to call 30th Celebration the most-hyped Pokémon TCG set of all time.

Releasing on Wednesday, September 16, 2026 all across the world, 30th Celebration represents the culmination of an unprecedented year for Pokémon cards. With the popularity of Pokémon cards reaching never-before-seen heights in 2026, 30th Celebration is channeling all of that excitement and expectation into a single expansion. More people are opening Pokémon cards than ever before, and this is the set they most want to rip.

So, which cards are fans hoping to find in 30th Celebration? The honest answer is simply, "all of them." With its tidy set size, historical significance, and seemingly generous pull rates, 30th Celebration practically demands to be collected into master sets containing one of every card in the expansion. Some pulls will be rarer than others, but each one will be a crucial piece in somebody's collection, and every rarity contains cards with special significance.

For example: did you notice that the Rares in 30th Celebration are the 18 Legendary mascot Pokémon from the nine generations of Pokémon games? (With Mew and Mewtwo subbed in for Gen I.)

But it's tough to hold "everything" in your head while you're ripping packs. So to help you organize your Keep and Trade piles this week, we've put together a list of a few extra-special cards that fans are eager to get their hands on. These are the cards that everybody wants from the Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration set.

#10 Unown

The Common-rarity Unown won't be on most collectors' radars. If you're a player though, its Mysterious Signal attack may already be giving you flashbacks to meta-defining cards like Iron Hands ex and Arceus & Dialga & Palkia-GX.

Any Pokémon card that lets you cheat ahead in the Prize trade has a good chance of being busted. Mysterious Signal will have trouble getting there on its own most of the time (though its 40 damage is more than enough to one-shot Budew), but in combination with cards that let you spread damage counters, it can turn around an otherwise unwinnable game.

Keep an eye out for copies of this simple Common as you're ripping packs of 30th Celebration. You may want to keep it for yourself if you like mingo's colorful art, or the way the Unown spell out "anniversary." If not, you can probably find a player at your local game store who'll be happy to trade for it.

#9 The Yuka Morii Item Cards

Since 1998, Morii has set herself apart as a Pokémon card artist by using a unique medium. Instead of illustrating Pokémon, she sculpts them out of clay and photographs them using practical backgrounds, often in nature. 

With over 200 cards to her name, odds are high that you've encountered a Morii card yourself in the wild. But this is her first time lending her beloved style to highly playable Item cards like Poké Pad and Ultra Ball, both of which are basically mandatory to compete in Standard.

Collectors who follow Yuka Morii's work will need all three of these Item cards asap, and more than a few players will want to swap Morii's Item cards into all their decks going forward. Every player who needs a playset creates the same demand as four collectors who want one each, so there's a decent chance that these Item cards will be more valuable than you'd expect. If you're not planning to play with them, it won't be hard to find someone who is.

#8 Every "Pikachu Rare" Pikachu

Every booster pack of 30th Celebration comes with one of 30 unique "Pikachu Rare" cards, each featuring a different artist's take on the world's foremost electric mouse. Because they're numbered out of 30, fans will naturally want to collect 'em all, making them all more valuable by association.

Especially in the early days of 30th Celebration, everyone's first priority will be finding their personal favorite Pikachu Rare. The internet fell in love with OKACHEKE's squishy-cheeked Pikachu early on during the reveals of 30th Celebration, so that one's going to be especially sought-after. But fans may also gravitate toward Pikachu 12/30 by USGMEN, the artist behind Bubble Mew. Or Ken Sugimori's redraw of his iconic Pikachu from Base Set. Or the trippy Pikachu by fan-favorite artist Shinji Kanda.

Whatever Pikachu Rare you pull, it's going to be the exact one someone else is looking for.

#7 The Illustration Rare Legendary Birds

Some of the most desirable Pokémon cards of the 2020s have been connected art cards, where each card forms a piece of a larger illustration. And in 30th Celebration, we're getting a triptych of the most iconic Pokémon trio of all time.

The three Kanto Legendary Birds each have an Illustration Rare in 30th Celebration, which combine to form a colorful cloudscape illustration by mashu, the same artist behind the Bulbasaur connected artwork trio from Mega Evolution. 

Articuno, Zapdos, and Moltres have appeared as a connected art trio before, way back in 2009's Supreme Victors. Those are now some of the most valuable cards the legendary birds have ever received, which should give you a good indication of how popular these new connected art cards will be.

#6 Special Illustration Rare Greninja ex

With most modern Pokémon sets, the top of everyone's wishlist is filled with Special Illustration Rares (SIRs), the highest-rarity cards that spotlight each artist's unique style and each Pokémon's unique personality. 30th Celebration includes even more high-rarity prizes to chase than a typical set, but it's still chock-full of gorgeous SIRs that collectors are eager to find.

Other SIRs in 30th Celebration like Sylveon ex might end up carrying a higher price, but the Special Illustration Rare that everybody wants is Greninja ex. Not only has Greninja sneaked its way into the upper echelons of many Pokémon popularity polls, but this card's Stealthy Slash attack can assassinate Benched Pokémon out of nowhere, making this card an exciting find for players and collectors alike.

#5 Classic Collection Gengar (Prime)

Back in 2021, when Pokémon was celebrating its 25th year, the anniversary set Celebrations commemorated that history with a special subset called Classic Collection. This subset consisted of 25 iconic cards from the history of the Pokémon TCG, reprinted in their original style with the 25th anniversary logo.

Five years later, we're getting a new Classic Collection as a 30-card subset in 30th Celebration.

Most of the reprints this time weren't included in the Classic Collection five years ago, so only time will tell which ones end up being the most popular. Will it be the reprint of Shinji Kanda's Magikarp, which outperformed everyone's expectations to become the top chase card in Paldea Evolved? Or the reprint of Shining Celebi, whose original version goes for thousands of dollars?

For my money, we should expect great things from Gengar Prime. Every Gengar card on the market has been on an absolute tear over the past three years, including the original Gengar Prime, which went from $100 at the beginning of 2024 to over $1000 today. Heck, Gengar's so popular that people have tried to sell cards from other games by misidentifying it. No Gengar card can be overlooked in today's market.

#4 Day and Night Special Illustration Rare Pikachu ex

Earlier this year, the internet went a little nuts over Pokémon cards that featured "cameos" by other Pokémon who aren't included in the card's name.

The Pokémon Company sure knows how to please its audience. These two cards represent the entire 30th Celebration set in microcosm, complete with all the big-name Pokémon who're present in the set, and the daytime/nighttime theme that runs through all of 30th Celebration's visuals. With literally dozens of cameos, these SIRs form a natural capstone to 30th Celebration.

But every good concert has an encore, and 30th Celebration has a few chase cards that go beyond the set's "natural" apex.

#3 Classic Collection Charizard

Most of the cards in the 30th Celebration Classic Collection haven't been reprinted since their original set. But one card had to be the exception.

It wouldn't be a Pokémon anniversary set without an homage to Base Set Charizard, possibly the most famous trading card in history. Finding (and likely losing) this card sparked a lifelong obsession with Pokémon cards in an entire generation of fans. Decades later, we're still swimming through the wake this card left behind.

Nobody can return to the past, but we can tear open a fresh card wrapper in 2026 and find Mitsuhiro Arita's iconic illustration roaring back at us. No Pokémon fan will want to leave 30th Celebration behind before they've experienced that. 

#2 Futuristic Rare Mewtwo ex

Anniversaries are a time to look forward as well as back. To celebrate what might come in the next 30+ years of the Pokémon TCG, TPCi commissioned famed Japanese artist YOSHIROTTEN to define the look for a new rarity: Futuristic Rare.

(Personally, these don't look very "futuristic" to me. But I appreciate them more with the context of YOSHIROTTEN's 2018 FUTURE NATURE exhibition, which used the extremes of the visible spectrum to explore the theme of "seeing the invisible.") 

Fans have been waiting for these cards since Pokémon Day 2026 in February, before this anniversary set had a name. We don't yet know how hard they'll be to pull, but if The Pokémon Company follows the precedent set by similar one-off rarities like Black White Rare, Futuristic Rares will be extremely scarce—and therefore, valuable.

#1 Futuristic Rare Mew ex

While either of Futuristic Rares in 30th Celebration will be incredible pulls, Mew ex will likely be the more desirable of the two. Part of that comes down to its brighter color scheme, and to the way Mew has come to symbolize "the unobtainable" for Pokéman fans, as the only Gen I Pokémon that couldn't be captured by playing the original video games normally.

It also helps that Mew ex is the strongest new card in 30th Celebration. With its Memory Helix Ability, Mew ex can copy the attacks of any three-Prize Mega Pokémon ex while only giving up two Prizes itself. That's the same kind of Prize-cheating that makes Unown so dangerous, on a Pokémon that can slot easily into decks of any Energy type.

Editor's Note: This article originally ended here, but The Pokémon Company kept one more group of cards a secret until 30th Celebration released. Now that they've been revealed, the cards that everybody most wants from 30th Celebration are...

#0 The Three RGB Mew Cards

Like Mew itself in the original video games, these cards were originally just sketchy-sounding rumors. As early as July, a streamer opening 30th Celebration packs appeared to find a parallel Mew card with art credited to YOSHIROTTEN and a collector number of B/RGB.

This sparked a small firestorm of controversy over whether the card was actually real. Skeptics noted that the card didn't have the 30th Anniversary stamp common to all the other cards in both 30th Celebration and the 30th Celebration Classic Collection.

Now, the skeptics (myself among them) have to eat their words. The number of copies that have been found around the world are too numerous and similar to one another to be faked. While Mew R/RGB, Mew G/RGB, and Mew B/RGB have yet to be added to Pokémon's official card database or 30th Celebration marketing pages, it appears that The Pokémon Company just wants to keep an air of mystery around these exceptionally rare cards.

As Pokémon's best-kept secret in decades, the RGB Mew cards are the ultimate chase cards of 30th Celebration.
